newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Ousted Zaire cabinet says Mobutu must go.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Zaire cabinet says Mobutu must go.

text.p: The ousted government of radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi accused Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko of treason on Thursday and urged Zaireans to intensify pressure to force him from power.
At the same time, a spokesman for the veteran Mobutu foe urged Zaire's army to stop fighting Laurent Kabila's rebels, who already control half of the country including its economic heartland.

Earlier, Zaire's new military prime minister, presenting himself as the agent of an orderly transition, met diplomats and political leaders one day after Tshisekedi supporters and Mobutu's soldiers clashed in the capital.

Tshisekedi spokesman Joseph Yaone told reporters after a "cabinet" meeting in the ousted prime minister's garden that the ailing and embattled president should stand trial in the supreme court on charges of violating the constitution.
"Mr Mobutu, having illegally declared a state of emergency in Zaire, and appointed his prime minister illegally is guilty of high treason," Yaone said in a statement.

"We are appealing to the people to intensify pressure of all sorts in order to force Mr Mobutu from power," he added. "We are calling on the army to halt all fighting with the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire."
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and has dominated the sprawling Central African nation since then, is under growing international and domestic pressure to quit.
He declared a nationwide state of emergency on Tuesday and appointed military governors in areas still under central government control.
He shunted Tshisekedi aside on Wednesday, naming General Likulia Bolongo in what opponents say had all the hallmarks of a veiled coup.
"It's a coup d'etat reminiscent of 1960s when President Mobutu did whatever he wished," Alphonse Phongo, a senior Tshisekedi ally, commented.
Mobutu's army clashed on Wednesday with Tshisekedi loyalists trying to install their man in the prime minister's offices. The teeming capital was calm on Thursday, if quieter than usual.
Aides to Likulia, a former defence minister, told Reuters the general planned to spell out his programme.

"If peace reigns then we will govern normally," Likulia told a Wednesday night news conference. "If there is agitation, and behaviour that will disturb the functions of the state, it is normal that we will take the necessary measures."
These, he said, could be ... "police measures tending to restrict certain liberties".
The rebels, who took up arms against Mobutu in October, control half the country including diamond-rich Kasai and much of the southern copper and cobalt mining province of Shaba.
Likulia, in public at least, rejected suggestions that the veteran African strongman was looking for a dignified way out and had appointed him to smoothe his departure.

Mobutu, he said, would only go in accordance with the laws governing Zaire's much-delayed transition to democracy. "If in the first elections the head of state is defeated he will leave. But if he is re-elected he will continue."
Many Mobutu watchers and opponents remained unconvinced.
"It's a desperate bit of last-minute improvisation that can only spell the end of the Mobutu regime," Phongo commented.
